scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users opened ticket #4521: they can no longer reach the Server
Room (1.0.0.x) or Internet Lab (128.168.0.x). Their team has decided the
problem is router0 -- "router0 stopped routing for us" -- since router0 is the
gateway their traffic leaves through. Please confirm that router0 has stopped
routing and identify what failed on router0.

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath2-router1-ip-forward-off: router1 is not
forwarding transit traffic. A FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 makes it drop
every packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (the iptables equivalent of
net.ipv4.ip_forward=0). router1 is the only transit hop between the
192.168.x.x departments and the Server Room / Internet Lab, so IT/CS traffic
(it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2) is dropped at router1. The tell is
that office_pc, which sits on router1's OWN LAN, can still ping its gateway
192.168.3.1 (local delivery), but cannot reach the Server Room (transit) --
router1 is up but not forwarding.

The TWIST: the ticket blames router0 ("router0 stopped routing"). router0 is
HEALTHY -- its ripd is running, its RIP table is intact, its interfaces are up,
and it correctly forwards the IT/CS traffic onward to router1 over the serial
link. router0 is simply the users' first hop, so they accuse it; the packets
actually die one hop later, at router1's FORWARD-chain drop. This is classic
first-hop bias toward the users' own gateway.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router1 (packet
forwarding disabled / FORWARD-chain drop). The agent must localise from the
evidence -- router1 forwards local but not transit traffic -- and explicitly
NOT pin the fault on router0 despite the prompt. An agent that "confirms
router0 stopped routing" has followed the accusation instead of the evidence.
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1.
scoring_axes: must-identify-forwarding-disabled: router1 not forwarding transit (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward=0)
bonus-exonerates-router0: notes router0's ripd, routes, and interfaces are healthy and it correctly forwards onward

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router0 is routing correctly; the outage is caused by router1’s firewall dropping all transit traffic. Evidence on router0 shows normal routing: ip_forward=1, no restrictive iptables rules (FORWARD policy ACCEPT), correct RIP-learned routes to 1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 via 10.10.0.2, and it can reach router1 (ping 10.10.0.2 OK). IT/CS hosts can ping their default gateway (192.168.1.1/192.168.2.1) and even router1’s 10.10.0.2 address, proving router0 is forwarding to router1.

The symptom (IT/CS unable to reach Server Room or Internet Lab) occurs because traffic must transit router1 from 10.10.0.0/8 to 20.20.0.0/8 and onward. On router1, iptables shows “-A FORWARD -j DROP” with packet counters incrementing, while INPUT/OUTPUT are ACCEPT. Thus packets forwarded through router1 are dropped, but packets sourced by router1 (our tests pinging 1.0.0.5 and 128.168.0.3 from router1) still succeed. Router2’s inability to ping 192.168.1.x/192.168.2.x further confirms router1 is blocking transit.

Localization: router1, iptables FORWARD chain. Routing (RIP) and IP forwarding are otherwise healthy across all routers.

Root cause: an iptables rule on router1 (“-A FORWARD -j DROP”) that drops all forwarded packets.

Corrective fix: remove/adjust the firewall rule on router1. For example: iptables -D FORWARD 1 (or flush FORWARD chain), then implement proper allow/stateful rules (e.g., iptables -A FORWARD -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT; iptables -A FORWARD -i eth2 -o eth3 -j ACCEPT; iptables -A FORWARD -i eth3 -o eth2 -j ACCEPT) and persist the change. Router0 requires no changes.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-forwarding-disabled: router1 not forwarding transit (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward=0)
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies router1 as blocking transit traffic via an iptables ‘-A FORWARD -j DROP’ (i.e., forwarding disabled for transit), matching the required diagnosis.

per_axis.axis: bonus-exonerates-router0: notes router0's ripd, routes, and interfaces are healthy and it correctly forwards onward
per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly exonerates router0, citing ripd and routes are correct, ip_forward=1, interfaces up, and that router0 successfully forwards packets to router1 (ping/route evidence).
Correctly proposes removing the DROP in router1's FORWARD chain (e.g., iptables -D FORWARD, flush, then add stateful/allow rules and persist), which matches the expected fix.

The agent's log contains direct evidence (router1 iptables FORWARD drop, router0 ip_forward=1 and acceptable iptables, successful local pings, failed end-to-end pings) and the writeup's inferences follow from those observations. A few minor output truncations obscure some counter details, but the conclusion that router1 is dropping transit traffic is well supported.
